title: Obligation, Necessity & Permission (Extended): Rules, Advice and Rights
description: Distinguish strict mandates from recommendations and prohibitions, compare must versus have to, master formal may versus ability can, and analyse modals in real policy documents and everyday rules.
author: AST English Academy

props.content: Modal verbs tell the listener how much choice they have. A strict mandate leaves no room for debate — you must comply or face consequences. A recommendation guides you strongly but allows personal choice. A permission grants the right to act. A prohibition forbids an action entirely.

data: Drivers must stop at red traffic lights.
You should drink water during long workouts.
You must not enter without a permit.
Sixth-form students may leave campus at lunch.

props.title: Must Not vs Don't Have To
props.content: 'You must not smoke' = forbidden (prohibition). 'You don't have to smoke' = not required but allowed. These mean completely different things — never confuse them!

slides.title: Must vs Have To: External vs Internal

props.content: Both must and have to express obligation, but with a subtle difference. Must often reflects the speaker's own authority or a strong personal rule: 'I must finish this essay tonight.' Have to typically reflects an external rule or law: 'Employees have to wear ID badges.' In everyday modern English, they are often interchangeable for strict rules.

items.title: Can I use must and have to interchangeably?
items.content: For laws and school rules, yes: 'You must wear uniform' = 'You have to wear uniform.' In formal writing, 'must' sounds more authoritative.

items.title: How do I express lack of obligation?
items.content: Use 'don't have to' or 'needn't': 'You don't have to attend the meeting' means attendance is optional.

items.title: What about 'shall' for rules?
items.content: 'Shall' appears in very formal legal documents: 'The tenant shall pay rent on the first of each month.' It is rare in everyday speech.

props.statement: 'You don't have to bring a calculator' means bringing a calculator is forbidden.
props.explanation: 'Don't have to' means it is NOT obligatory — you may bring one if you wish, but it is optional. 'Must not bring' would mean forbidden.

slides.title: Should and Ought To: Advisory Modals

props.content: Should and ought to give advice or express what is morally or practically right — but the listener retains freedom to choose. Teachers, doctors, and parents use these constantly: 'You should revise every evening' is guidance, not a law. Ignoring advice may have consequences, but it is not the same as breaking a rule.

props.title: Mandate vs Advice — Compare the Force

cards.front: MANDATE: You must wear a helmet.
cards.back: Non-negotiable safety law. No helmet = no riding.

cards.front: ADVICE: You should wear a helmet.
cards.back: Strong recommendation. You can choose, but it is wise to comply.

cards.front: PROHIBITION: You must not run in the corridor.
cards.back: Absolutely forbidden. Running breaks a school rule.

cards.front: OPTIONAL: You don't have to join the club.
cards.back: Membership is voluntary — no obligation at all.

questions.question: Which sentence is advice rather than a strict rule?

options.text: Students should review notes each evening.
Students must not use phones in class.
Students have to wear school uniform.

questions.explanation: 'Should' expresses a recommendation, not a mandatory rule.

slides.title: May vs Can: Permission vs Ability

props.content: In formal English, may grants or requests official permission: 'May I ask a question?' In everyday speech, can often replaces 'may' for permission, but technically can describes physical or mental ability: 'She can run ten miles' means she has the capability. Using 'may' in exams and formal writing shows precision and courtesy.

data: May I leave the room? / You may begin the exam.
Can I borrow your pen? (everyday speech)
Could I use the printer, please?

props.content: Analyse Modals in a Code of Conduct

props.title: Tap Hotspots to Identify Mandates, Prohibitions, and Permissions

hotspots.label: Strict Requirement
hotspots.content: 'Students MUST wear full school uniform at all times.' Non-negotiable mandate with disciplinary consequences.

hotspots.label: Prohibition
hotspots.content: 'Mobile phones MUST NOT be used during lesson time.' Absolute prohibition — using a phone breaks this rule.

hotspots.label: Granted Permission
hotspots.content: 'Sixth-form students MAY leave campus during lunch hour.' Formal permission granted to a specific group.

hotspots.label: Recommendation
hotspots.content: 'All students SHOULD join at least one extracurricular club.' Encouraged but not compulsory.

props.statement: 'You may open your exam papers now' expresses formal permission, not physical ability.
props.explanation: 'May' here grants official permission from the examiner to begin. This is a formal context where 'may' is preferred over 'can'.

props.title: Match Modal Phrases to Their Legal and Social Function
The Three Most Common Errors
props.content: 1. Confusing 'must not' (forbidden) with 'don't have to' (optional). 2. Using 'can' when 'may' is required in formal permission. 3. Treating 'should' as a strict law instead of advice.

questions.explanation: 'Must not' and 'cannot' express prohibition. 'Should not' is advice. 'Don't have to' means optional.

props.content: Reading Modals in Signs, Policies, and Notices

Public signs and official documents rely heavily on modal verbs. A 'No Entry' sign implies must not enter. A 'Visitors Welcome' sign implies may enter. Learning to decode modals in real texts helps you understand your rights and responsibilities instantly.

questions.explanation: 'May I...?' is the formal standard for permission requests.

props.content: Obligation, Permission and Prohibition — Key Takeaways

props.text: Rules are not necessarily sacred, principles are.
props.author: Franklin D. Roosevelt

items: Must/have to = strict mandate; should/ought to = advice; may/can = permission; must not/cannot = prohibition.
Never confuse 'must not' (forbidden) with 'don't have to' (optional).
Use 'may' for formal permission; use 'can' for physical ability.
Policy documents, signs, and school rules all rely on precise modal choice.

questions.question: Which sentence expresses a PROHIBITION?
options: You must not run in the hall.
questions.explanation: 'Must not' forbids the action entirely — it is a prohibition.

questions.question: Which modal best fits a formal permission request?
questions.explanation: 'May I...?' is the standard formal permission request.
